title: Cop recalls canine partner's last minutes: Coroner's jury reviews video evidence
article: Const. Stephen Kaye is a big, strapping man with bulging arms and a square jaw. Climbing into the witness box at the inquest into the death of Keldon McMillan Wednesday, he looked unflappable.

But as he described watching his former partner and constant companion, the police dog Cyr, running through a darkened field toward the loaded gun in McMillan's hand on May 20, 2001, Kaye fell silent.
When he spoke again, his voice had begun to waver.

"Cyr got about six feet away and Mr. McMillan turned towards him and fired a single round into the dog." Wounded but still trying to do his job, the dog bit McMillan's arm and side, he told the jury. McMillan fired another bullet into Cyr before the dog finally fell and limped away.
"I assumed he was going to shoot me as well, (and) I realized I had nothing to hide behind," Kaye recalled. He began to run, emptying his service revolver in McMillan's direction as he went.

Kaye said he didn't know how many shots he'd fired until, running toward McMillan in the darkness, he realized his clip was empty. He thought he was the only one shooting, but McMillan had been felled by another city police officer with a shotgun and was lying on the ground.

The 33-year-old home builder raised his head and right hand, seeming to aim at him, Kaye said. The officer threw his empty gun away and jumped, landing with one foot on the man's head, the other on his gun hand. McMillan died seconds later.
Kaye was kneeling next to Cyr when the dog died.
Marty Minuk, the lawyer representing McMillan's family, theorized that McMillan was simply reacting to Cyr's approach when he quickly turned toward police with his gun.
Minuk would not say whether McMillan's family considers that an improper reaction by the police. Family members attending the inquest have declined comment.
Witnesses have differed in their testimony about who shot first - - McMillan or police -- following a high-speed chase from Saskatoon to a roadside turnout about seven kilometres south of Wakaw.

The six-member coroner's jury watched a four-minute video showing part of the confrontation Wednesday. Shot through the windshield of an RCMP cruiser, it shows McMillan standing next to his truck facing a city police cruiser, one hand casually on his hip and the other holding his gun.
He fires into the air, raises both hands beside his head, then lets them drop, turns and walks nonchalantly away from police spotlights into the darkness. Less than 30 seconds later, it was all over.
The inquest is expected to conclude Friday in Court of Queen's Bench.
